title: Bisulfid vs Bisulfide: Meanings, IUPAC Names and German Usage
summary: The two words look like one term in two spellings. The cited sources do not treat them that way: Merriam-Webster defines bisulfide as disulfide, PubChem lists bisulfide as a synonym for the hydrosulfide ion (HS⁻), and of the German dictionaries consulted, Duden and the DWDS define Sulfid while the DWDS reports that Bisulfid is not among its contemporary lexical sources.
reference_task: What do bisulfide (English) and Bisulfid (German) mean according to authoritative sources, which chemical species is each word attached to, and how do they relate to sulfide, disulfide and bisulfite?

at_a_glance.value: listed as a synonym of {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-HS-SYNONYMS:lexical.molecular_formula}}, record title {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-HS-SYNONYMS:lexical.record_title}} (CID {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-HS-SYNONYMS:lexical.cid}})

modules.heading: Bisulfide in Merriam-Webster: a cross-reference to disulfide

paragraphs.text: Merriam-Webster enters {{EVD-TERM-MW-BISULFIDE:lexical.headword}} as a {{EVD-TERM-MW-BISULFIDE:lexical.part_of_speech}} whose whole definition is a cross-reference: “{{EVD-TERM-MW-BISULFIDE:lexical.definition_quoted}}”. The dictionary dates its first known use to {{EVD-TERM-MW-BISULFIDE:lexical.first_known_use}}.
Read with the disulfide entry below, the dictionary sense of bisulfide is a compound with two sulfur atoms. The entry gives no sense that involves hydrogen.

modules.heading: Bisulfide in PubChem: a synonym listed for HS⁻

paragraphs.text: PubChem record CID {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-HS-SYNONYMS:lexical.cid}} has the formula {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-HS-SYNONYMS:lexical.molecular_formula}}, the computed IUPAC name {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-HS-SYNONYMS:lexical.computed_iupac_name}} and the title {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-HS-SYNONYMS:lexical.record_title}}, and its synonym list includes “{{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-HS-SYNONYMS:lexical.synonym_listed}}”.

The same English spelling therefore points to two different species in two kinds of source: the dictionary maps it to disulfide, two sulfur atoms, while the database attaches it to the hydrosulfide ion, one sulfur and one hydrogen. A synonym list records names that are in use; it is not a naming recommendation.

modules.heading: HS⁻ in IUPAC nomenclature: sulfanide or hydridosulfate(1−)

paragraphs.text: The IUPAC 2005 recommendations on inorganic nomenclature give the anion {{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-HS-NAMES:lexical.anion}} two names: {{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-HS-NAMES:lexical.substitutive_name}} as the substitutive name and {{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-HS-NAMES:lexical.additive_name}} as the additive name ({{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-HS-NAMES:lexical.section}}).
Bisulfide is not one of the names given in that example. Where precision matters, the IUPAC names identify HS⁻ without the ambiguity of the bi- form.

Merriam-Webster gives {{EVD-TERM-MW-DISULFIDE:lexical.headword}} two senses: “{{EVD-TERM-MW-DISULFIDE:lexical.sense_1_quoted}}” and “{{EVD-TERM-MW-DISULFIDE:lexical.sense_2_quoted}}”, with a first known use of {{EVD-TERM-MW-DISULFIDE:lexical.first_known_use}}.

For the anion {{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-S2-NAMES:lexical.anion}} the same recommendations give {{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-S2-NAMES:lexical.homopolyatomic_name}}, and {{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-S2-NAMES:lexical.parent_hydride_name}} on the parent-hydride basis ({{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-S2-NAMES:lexical.section}}).

Merriam-Webster defines {{EVD-TERM-MW-SULFIDE:lexical.headword}} in two senses: “{{EVD-TERM-MW-SULFIDE:lexical.sense_1_quoted}}”, and “{{EVD-TERM-MW-SULFIDE:lexical.sense_2_quoted}}”. Its first known use is {{EVD-TERM-MW-SULFIDE:lexical.first_known_use}}.

modules.heading: Bisulfite: a different word, defined through sulfite

paragraphs.text: Merriam-Webster defines {{EVD-TERM-MW-BISULFITE:lexical.headword}} as “{{EVD-TERM-MW-BISULFITE:lexical.definition_quoted}}”, first known use {{EVD-TERM-MW-BISULFITE:lexical.first_known_use}}.
Bisulfite is one letter away from bisulfide, but the dictionary defines it through sulfite, not sulfide. The two words should not be used interchangeably.

For {{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-HSO3-NAME:lexical.anion}} IUPAC accepts the abbreviated name {{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-HSO3-NAME:lexical.accepted_abbreviated_name}}; the full hydrogen name is {{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-HSO3-NAME:lexical.full_hydrogen_name}} ({{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-HSO3-NAME:lexical.section}}). IUPAC adds: “{{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-HSO3-NAME:lexical.list_status_quoted}}”.

PubChem record CID {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-BISULFITE:lexical.cid}}, titled {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-BISULFITE:lexical.record_title}}, has the formula {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-BISULFITE:lexical.molecular_formula}} and the computed IUPAC name {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-BISULFITE:lexical.computed_iupac_name}}.
The database therefore places bisulfite on an oxygen-containing anion, not on any sulfide.

modules.heading: Sulfid in Duden and the DWDS

paragraphs.text: Duden defines {{EVD-TERM-DUDEN-SULFID:lexical.headword}} as “{{EVD-TERM-DUDEN-SULFID:lexical.definition_quoted}}”. The DWDS entry (source: {{EVD-TERM-DWDS-SULFID:lexical.dictionary}}) labels the word {{EVD-TERM-DWDS-SULFID:lexical.domain_label}} and defines it as “{{EVD-TERM-DWDS-SULFID:lexical.definition_quoted}}”.

Both German definitions are given in terms of hydrogen sulfide, like the second English sense of sulfide above. For this pair the evidence shows a spelling difference with a matching definition; that finding does not carry over to other pairs such as Bisulfid and bisulfide.

modules.heading: Hydrogensulfid in a German chemistry lexicon

paragraphs.text: In its entry {{EVD-TERM-SPEKTRUM-HYDROGENSULFIDE:lexical.entry}}, the Spektrum chemistry lexicon states that hydrogen sulfide forms two series of salts: {{EVD-TERM-SPEKTRUM-HYDROGENSULFIDE:lexical.salt_series|valence}}.
In this German reference work the salts of HS⁻ are called Hydrogensulfide. The passage does not use the word Bisulfid.

modules.heading: Bisulfid in the DWDS: not among its contemporary lexical sources

paragraphs.text: For {{EVD-TERM-DWDS-BISULFID:lexical.headword}} the DWDS answers: “{{EVD-TERM-DWDS-BISULFID:lexical.coverage_statement_quoted}}” It shows {{EVD-TERM-DWDS-BISULFID:lexical.forms_shown}}.
The DWDS gives the same answer for {{EVD-TERM-DWDS-HYDROGENSULFID:lexical.headword}}: “{{EVD-TERM-DWDS-HYDROGENSULFID:lexical.coverage_statement_quoted}}”

Missing from one dictionary's contemporary sources is not the same as never used. It shows only that the DWDS does not record the word; it cannot settle what Bisulfid refers to, and it says nothing about other dictionaries or technical texts.

modules.heading: The German -id ending: a naming pattern, not proof of a standard term

paragraphs.text: A German university teaching text on inorganic nomenclature states the rule: “{{EVD-TERM-FHM-ID-RULE:lexical.rule_quoted}}” Its table of monatomic anions lists the sulfide ion as “{{EVD-TERM-FHM-ID-RULE:lexical.example_row}}”.
The rule explains the spelling Sulfid. It does not say what Bisulfid refers to, and none of the dictionaries or nomenclature sources cited here defines Bisulfid.

not_established.heading: What this reference does not establish
not_established.text: BISULFID is the name of this website. The name is not a chemical claim, and this reference does not state that German Bisulfid is the equivalent of English bisulfide. One captured industry page uses Bisulfid in connection with HS⁻, but an industry page is not admissible as evidence of standardized German terminology here. This observation is retained as a boundary; it cannot establish general usage or a recommended name. The IUPAC Gold Book entry on hydrosulfides could not be retrieved openly when the sources were captured, and a second German teaching handout was unreachable, so neither is cited. Other German dictionaries were not examined for Bisulfid. The history of the bi- prefix, how often each spelling is used, and the safety or industrial properties of any species named here are outside this reference [SOURCE REQUIRED].

synthesis.heading: What the sources support, what stays open, and what not to infer
synthesis.intro: Each statement below draws only on the evidence cited in brackets. It separates what a dictionary, a nomenclature standard, a database and a technical lexicon each record, because they answer different questions.

items.text: In Merriam-Webster, bisulfide is a cross-reference to disulfide, whose first sense is “{{EVD-TERM-MW-DISULFIDE:lexical.sense_1_quoted}}”.

In PubChem, bisulfide is one of the synonyms listed for {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-HS-SYNONYMS:lexical.molecular_formula}}, the record titled {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-HS-SYNONYMS:lexical.record_title}} with the computed IUPAC name {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-HS-SYNONYMS:lexical.computed_iupac_name}}.

IUPAC's 2005 recommendations name HS⁻ {{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-HS-NAMES:lexical.substitutive_name}} or {{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-HS-NAMES:lexical.additive_name}}, and S₂²⁻ {{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-S2-NAMES:lexical.homopolyatomic_name}}; bisulfide is not among the names given in those examples.

German Sulfid and the inorganic sense of English sulfide are both defined in terms of hydrogen sulfide: “{{EVD-TERM-DWDS-SULFID:lexical.definition_quoted}}” (DWDS) and “a salt of hydrogen sulfide” (Merriam-Webster).
In the German chemistry lexicon consulted, the salts of HS⁻ are called Hydrogensulfide; the passage does not use the word Bisulfid.

Bisulfite names an oxygen-containing anion, {{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-HSO3-NAME:lexical.anion}} ({{EVD-TERM-IUPAC-HSO3-NAME:lexical.accepted_abbreviated_name}}); PubChem titles that record {{EVD-TERM-PUBCHEM-BISULFITE:lexical.record_title}}.

groups.label: Open: the cited sources do not settle it

items.text: Which species a given writer means by bisulfide. The sources attach the word to two different species, disulfide (dictionary) and HS⁻ (database synonym), so only the context of a text can decide.
Whether Bisulfid is established German usage. The DWDS does not record it in its contemporary sources, and no admissible terminology source for German usage has been found yet.

groups.label: Not to be inferred from similar spelling

items.text: That Bisulfid is the standardized German equivalent of bisulfide. The German -id ending is a naming pattern: it explains a spelling, not which species a word denotes.
That bisulfide and bisulfite are interchangeable because they differ by one letter. One is defined through disulfide, the other through sulfite.
That an absence from the DWDS means an absence from every German dictionary or technical text.
